name: Arrays & Hashing
checklist: Ask if array is sorted
Consider hash map for complement/frequency lookup
Watch for O(n^2) brute force you can collapse to O(n)
mistakes: Reaching for nested loops before considering a map
Not handling duplicate keys/values correctly

name: Two Pointers
checklist: Sort first if order doesn't matter
Move the pointer on the 'worse' side
Handle duplicates by skipping equal adjacent values
mistakes: Forgetting to skip duplicates in 3Sum-style problems
Off-by-one when pointers cross

name: Sliding Window
checklist: Expand right pointer
Check if window is invalid
Shrink left until valid again
Update answer at the right point (usually after shrinking)
mistakes: Updating the answer before shrinking back to valid
Forgetting to remove zero-count entries from the frequency map
Using a fixed-size window pattern for a variable-size problem

name: Stack
checklist: Decide monotonic increasing vs decreasing
Pop while the condition is violated before pushing
Track indices, not just values, when you need distances
mistakes: Pushing values when you need indices
Not popping everything at the end for 'remaining' elements

name: Binary Search
recognize: Monotonic answer space ('can we do X with capacity Y?')
checklist: Define search space and what 'true'/'false' means at a value
Use while l <= r for exact match, l < r for boundary search
Compute mid as l + (r-l)/2 to avoid overflow
mistakes: Infinite loop from wrong l/r update
Off-by-one between l <= r and l < r templates
Not recognizing a monotonic-answer binary search (binary search on the answer)

name: Linked List
checklist: Use a dummy head node for edge cases at the start
Draw the pointer rewiring before coding
Consider fast/slow pointers for cycle or middle-node problems
mistakes: Losing the reference to the next node before rewiring
Forgetting to handle empty list or single-node list

name: Trees
checklist: Decide recursive (top-down or bottom-up) vs iterative with a stack/queue
Define clearly what each recursive call returns
Consider level-order (BFS) when the problem is about levels/width
mistakes: Conflating top-down (pass state down) with bottom-up (return state up) designs
Not handling null nodes explicitly

name: BST
checklist: Use the in-order traversal = sorted sequence property
Prune one subtree instead of searching both when possible
For validation, pass down (min, max) bounds
mistakes: Validating BST by only comparing to immediate children instead of ancestor bounds
Ignoring the O(log n) advantage and treating it like a generic tree

name: Trie
checklist: Node = map of children + isEndOfWord flag
Insert/search both walk character by character
Consider a trie whenever repeated prefix work would be wasteful with a hash set
mistakes: Forgetting the isEndOfWord flag (breaks prefix vs full-word distinction)
Using a fixed 26-array child map when the alphabet isn't just lowercase a-z

name: Heap / Priority Queue
checklist: Decide min-heap vs max-heap based on what you're evicting
For 'top K', keep a heap of size K, not size N
Consider a heap when you repeatedly need the current min/max after updates
mistakes: Using a max-heap of size N when a min-heap of size K is O(n log k) better
Forgetting Python's heapq is min-heap only (negate for max-heap)

name: Backtracking
checklist: Choose → explore → un-choose (backtrack) on every recursive branch
Prune early when a partial state can't lead to a valid answer
Track visited state and undo it after recursing
mistakes: Forgetting to undo state (visited flags, current path) after the recursive call
Not pruning, causing avoidable exponential blowup

name: Graph BFS
checklist: Use a queue and mark visited at enqueue time (not dequeue time)
Track distance/level alongside each node
Consider multi-source BFS when multiple valid starting points
mistakes: Marking visited on dequeue instead of enqueue, causing duplicate work
Using BFS when the graph is weighted (should be Dijkstra instead)

name: Graph DFS
checklist: Mark visited before/at recursion to avoid infinite loops
Recursive DFS vs iterative with an explicit stack (watch recursion depth)
For directed graphs, track 'in current path' separately from 'visited' to detect cycles
mistakes: Stack overflow on deep/recursive DFS for large inputs — consider iterative
Not distinguishing 'visited overall' from 'visited in current recursion path' for cycle detection

name: Union Find
checklist: Implement with path compression + union by rank/size
find() should recursively compress the path to the root
A cycle exists if union() is called on two nodes already in the same set
mistakes: Skipping path compression/union by rank, degrading to O(n) per operation
Forgetting union find is for undirected connectivity, not directed reachability

name: Topological Sort
recognize: Any 'ordering that respects a DAG' requirement
checklist: Kahn's algorithm: track in-degree, process nodes with in-degree 0
Or DFS-based: post-order the nodes, then reverse
A cycle exists if you can't process all nodes (result length < node count)
mistakes: Not detecting the cycle case (assuming the graph is always a valid DAG)
Confusing edge direction — 'a before b' means an edge a → b

name: DP 1D
recognize: Optimal value depends on a running decision (take/skip)
Climbing stairs / house robber / coin change style
State reducible to a single index
checklist: Define dp[i] precisely in words before coding
Write the recurrence relation from the definition
Consider rolling the array down to O(1) space once it works
mistakes: Vague dp[i] definition leading to a wrong recurrence
Off-by-one in base cases (dp[0], dp[1])

name: DP 2D
recognize: Two sequences being compared (edit distance, LCS)
State needs two indices to describe
checklist: Define dp[i][j] precisely before coding
Fill order matters — know which cells must be computed first
Consider compressing to two 1D rows if only the previous row is needed
mistakes: Wrong iteration order causing use of an uncomputed cell
Not handling the empty-prefix (row/col 0) base cases

name: Greedy
recognize: Local optimal choice seems to lead to global optimal
Problem says 'maximize/minimize' with an obvious sorting order
checklist: Sort by the criterion that makes the greedy choice obvious
Prove (even informally) that greedy doesn't miss a better global solution
If greedy fails on an example, it's probably a DP problem instead
mistakes: Assuming greedy works without checking a counterexample
Sorting by the wrong key (e.g., start time vs end time)

name: Intervals
checklist: Sort by start (or end, depending on the problem) first
Overlap condition: current.start <= previous.end
For 'minimum rooms/resources', consider a min-heap of end times or a sweep line
mistakes: Forgetting to sort before merging
Using <= vs < incorrectly at the overlap boundary
